difficultyReason: Statistical paradox requiring a self-selection explanation: patients who seek out experimental treatment may have more severe disease, masking the drug's real benefit. Distractors plausibly explain one horn only.
stimulus: Participants in a clinical trial who voluntarily enrolled in an experimental cancer drug program had a 20 percent lower five-year survival rate than cancer patients in the general population who received standard treatment. Yet the drug has been shown in laboratory settings to be significantly more effective at destroying cancer cells than any currently approved therapy.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy in the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The experimental drug has fewer side effects than most currently approved cancer therapies.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Patients who enrolled in the experimental program were, on average, diagnosed at a significantly more advanced stage of cancer than patients in the general population receiving standard treatment.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Laboratory conditions do not perfectly replicate the environment of the human body.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The experimental drug was administered at several hospitals across different regions.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Some patients in the general population also received experimental treatments not captured by the standard-treatment statistics.

explanations.correct: If trial enrollees had more advanced cancer at diagnosis, their lower survival rate reflects disease severity rather than drug inefficacy. The drug can be genuinely superior in destroying cancer cells while still failing to overcome the disadvantage of later-stage disease — dissolving the apparent conflict.
explanations.A: Side-effect profiles do not explain why the drug's superior cell-destruction ability fails to produce better survival rates in the trial group. This resolves neither horn.
explanations.B: Correct. Self-selection into the trial by sicker patients explains the survival gap without contradicting the lab evidence.
explanations.C: This weakens the lab evidence rather than reconciling the two facts; it deepens rather than resolves the paradox.
explanations.D: Geographic breadth of administration is irrelevant to explaining the survival-rate discrepancy.
explanations.E: This potentially narrows the gap in the comparison group but does not explain why experimental-drug patients fared worse, leaving the paradox intact.

difficultyReason: Economic paradox: a city raises the minimum wage but poverty rates rise. Resolution requires a confounding labor-market variable (employment loss). Distractors target one horn or deepen the paradox.
stimulus: A major city raised its minimum wage by 30 percent over three years, intending to reduce poverty among low-income workers. Despite this increase, the city's official poverty rate rose by four percentage points during the same period, even as the regional economy as a whole was expanding.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to explain the surprising outcome described above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Workers who retained their jobs at the new minimum wage earned substantially more than they had previously.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The city's poverty threshold is calculated using a formula that has remained unchanged for decades.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Many low-wage employers in the city reduced hours or eliminated entry-level positions in response to the wage increase, leaving thousands of previously employed workers without income.

choices.label: D
choices.text: City residents at all income levels reported greater satisfaction with their financial situations after the wage increase took effect.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The regional economy's expansion was driven primarily by high-technology industries that employ very few minimum-wage workers.

explanations.correct: If the wage hike caused employers to eliminate jobs, the workers who lost employment would have no income at all — pushing the poverty rate up despite the remaining workers earning more. This reconciles both facts: wages rose and poverty rose simultaneously.
explanations.A: This explains why some workers benefited but does not account for why overall poverty increased. It resolves one horn only.
explanations.B: An outdated formula could distort the poverty measurement, but the answer does not specify how this would cause the measured rate to rise, making it too vague to resolve the paradox.
explanations.C: Correct. Job losses due to the wage hike provide the confounding mechanism that explains rising poverty despite higher wages.
explanations.D: Self-reported satisfaction contradicts rather than explains a rising poverty rate, and actually deepens the paradox.
explanations.E: This context about tech expansion tells us the broader economy doesn't directly help low-wage workers, but it does not explain the mechanism by which poverty increased — it resolves one horn only.

difficultyReason: Environmental-science paradox: a river's fish population declined after a factory closed. Resolution via reverse causation/alternative mechanism (a competing stressor). Distractors explain closure consequences but not the fish decline.
stimulus: After a chemical manufacturing plant on the Aldren River closed its operations, discharge of industrial pollutants into the river ceased entirely. Yet within two years of the closure, the river's native fish population had declined by nearly 40 percent compared to pre-closure levels.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy in the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The plant had employed a water-treatment process that, as a byproduct, maintained elevated oxygen levels in the river downstream of the facility.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Fish populations in rivers without chemical plants also fluctuate from year to year due to seasonal changes.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Environmental regulators conducted water-quality tests for two years after the plant closed and found no remaining chemical contamination.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The chemical plant had operated on the Aldren River for more than fifty years before its closure.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Fish in the Aldren River had developed partial resistance to the chemicals previously discharged by the plant.

explanations.correct: If the plant's water-treatment process was inadvertently oxygenating the river and that byproduct disappeared with the closure, fish habitat quality may have worsened despite the elimination of chemical pollution — reconciling cleaner water with a declining fish population.
explanations.A: Correct. A hidden beneficial byproduct of the plant that vanished upon closure explains why removing pollution still led to worse ecological outcomes.
explanations.B: Normal year-to-year fluctuations cannot account for a 40-percent decline following a specific event; this is irrelevant to the paradox.
explanations.C: Confirming the absence of residual chemicals actually deepens the paradox: if the water is clean, why are fish declining?
explanations.D: The plant's operating history does not explain the post-closure decline; this is irrelevant to the paradox.
explanations.E: Partial resistance to chemicals that are no longer present does not explain the decline — it resolves neither horn of the paradox.

difficultyReason: Technology paradox: users who receive spam filters get more unwanted email. Self-selection/reverse causation: filters attract heavy email users. Distractors sound plausible but address only one horn.
stimulus: Users of a major email service who opted into the provider's new AI-powered spam filter received, on average, 35 percent more unwanted commercial emails per month than users who did not activate the filter. Yet internal tests conducted by the provider confirmed that the filter accurately blocks over 95 percent of detected spam.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy in the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Users who activated the spam filter were primarily heavy email users who had already subscribed to far more commercial mailing lists than average users.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The spam filter was offered free of charge to all users of the email service.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Spam filters from competing email providers perform at similar accuracy rates to the provider's new AI filter.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The provider's internal testing was conducted on a sample of emails specifically curated to represent a wide variety of spam types.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Some users who activated the filter subsequently reported feeling less concerned about email security.

explanations.correct: If users who opted in were already receiving far more spam-eligible emails due to extensive mailing-list subscriptions, the 35-percent excess reflects a pre-existing differential in exposure rather than filter failure. Even a 95-percent-effective filter leaves more spam reaching heavy users than lightly subscribed non-filter users receive in total.
explanations.A: Correct. Self-selection explains that the filter group had far greater baseline spam exposure, reconciling the outcome data with the filter's proven accuracy.
explanations.B: The cost of the filter is irrelevant to whether it works or why filtered users receive more spam.
explanations.C: Competitor performance does not explain the internal discrepancy; this is irrelevant.
explanations.D: Test methodology explains the 95-percent figure but does not account for why filter users receive more unwanted email — it resolves one horn only.
explanations.E: Changed user attitudes may suggest behavioral changes, but no mechanism linking reduced concern to more spam received is established; too speculative to resolve the paradox.

difficultyReason: Policy paradox: speed cameras in school zones reduced speeding but increased pedestrian injuries. Hidden mechanism (driver attention distraction) explains both. Distractors deepen or address only one horn.
stimulus: After a city installed speed cameras in all school zones, the percentage of drivers exceeding the posted speed limit dropped from 42 percent to 11 percent. Nevertheless, the number of pedestrian injuries in those same school zones increased by 18 percent in the year following camera installation.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy in the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Speed cameras of the type installed by the city have been used successfully in other jurisdictions to reduce pedestrian fatalities.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Many drivers, upon noticing the cameras, slowed abruptly and then directed their attention toward the camera rather than toward the road, causing a sharp increase in distraction-related collisions.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The school zones where cameras were installed had historically lower pedestrian-injury rates than zones without cameras.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Pedestrian injuries in school zones without cameras remained unchanged during the same period.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Drivers who received speeding fines from the cameras tended to challenge them in administrative hearings.

explanations.correct: If cameras caused drivers to brake suddenly and look away from the road, a new form of collision risk emerged that offset the benefit of lower speeds. This accounts for both facts: fewer speeders yet more injuries, because driver distraction became the new hazard.
explanations.A: Evidence that cameras work elsewhere actually deepens the paradox — if they work in other cities, why do injuries rise here?
explanations.B: Correct. Camera-induced distraction introduces a confounding mechanism that explains rising injuries despite falling speeding rates.
explanations.C: Lower historical injury rates in camera zones set up a regression-to-the-mean possibility but do not explain the post-installation increase; this resolves one horn only.
explanations.D: Stable injuries in non-camera zones confirm the camera zones worsened but do not explain why — this deepens rather than resolves the paradox.
explanations.E: Administrative challenges to fines are irrelevant to pedestrian injury rates.

difficultyReason: Linguistics paradox: a language-immersion program improves test scores but students show weaker everyday conversational fluency. Resolution requires a definitional/measurement distinction (tests measure formal accuracy; conversation requires informal register). Distractors address only one metric.
stimulus: Students enrolled in an intensive foreign-language immersion program scored, on average, 22 points higher on standardized proficiency exams than students who received traditional classroom instruction. Yet teachers and native speakers who interacted with immersion students consistently rated those students' conversational fluency as noticeably weaker than that of traditionally taught students at the same proficiency-exam level.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy in the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The standardized proficiency exams used in the comparison focus exclusively on formal grammar, reading comprehension, and written composition, and do not assess informal spoken registers or colloquial expression.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Immersion programs are generally more expensive to operate than traditional classroom instruction.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Some immersion students had prior exposure to the language before enrolling in the program.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Native speakers tend to rate non-native conversational fluency more harshly than trained language teachers do.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Traditional classroom instruction incorporates more hours of writing practice than immersion programs typically provide.

explanations.correct: If proficiency exams measure only formal written skills and immersion training emphasizes those same formal skills, immersion students can score higher on exams while still being weaker in the informal conversational register that native speakers and teachers are actually evaluating. The two metrics measure different things, dissolving the apparent conflict.
explanations.A: Correct. A definitional/measurement mismatch between what the exam tests and what conversational fluency requires reconciles both halves of the paradox.
explanations.B: Program cost is irrelevant to the discrepancy between exam scores and conversational ratings.
explanations.C: Prior exposure could inflate immersion students' scores, but it does not explain why their conversational fluency is weaker relative to score-matched traditionally taught students.
explanations.D: If native speakers rate everyone more harshly, this does not explain why immersion students are rated lower than traditionally taught students at the same score level — it resolves neither horn.
explanations.E: Greater writing practice in traditional programs would predict lower immersion exam scores, not higher — this actually deepens the paradox.

difficultyReason: Historical paradox: a medieval city's population grew rapidly during a period of documented famine. Temporal/contextual resolution: refugees from worse-affected regions inflated local numbers. Distractors address only the famine or only the growth.
stimulus: Historical records show that the city of Velmoor experienced its fastest population growth during the decade-long famine of the 1340s, when grain harvests across the region failed repeatedly and the death toll in surrounding villages was catastrophic. Yet Velmoor's own grain stores were reported by contemporary chroniclers to be no better supplied than those of the surrounding areas.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy in the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Velmoor was a walled city, which gave its residents a sense of security unavailable to inhabitants of surrounding open villages.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Survivors from the devastated surrounding villages fled to Velmoor in such large numbers that immigration exceeded the city's own famine mortality, producing a net population increase.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The famine of the 1340s was less severe in Velmoor than in any other location in the region.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Velmoor's chroniclers were known to exaggerate the city's prosperity in their written records.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Population counts in medieval cities were typically conducted by ecclesiastical authorities rather than civic officials.

explanations.correct: If large-scale refugee immigration to Velmoor outpaced famine deaths within the city, the net population would rise despite identical food scarcity conditions. This reconciles rapid growth with equally bad grain supplies: the city grew not because conditions were better but because outsiders arrived faster than insiders died.
explanations.A: A sense of security from walls may explain why refugees chose Velmoor, but the answer must explain actual population growth — this alone is insufficient and resolves one horn only.
explanations.B: Correct. Immigration exceeding internal mortality is the confounding mechanism that reconciles population growth with dire food conditions.
explanations.C: This directly contradicts the stimulus, which states Velmoor's supplies were no better than surrounding areas — this answer presupposes the opposite of what is given.
explanations.D: If chroniclers exaggerated prosperity, the grain-store data may be unreliable, but this undermines the stimulus rather than resolving the paradox within its given facts.
explanations.E: The method of census-taking is irrelevant to whether population actually grew during a famine.

difficultyReason: Law/policy paradox: mandatory sentencing laws reduced recidivism rates among released offenders but total crime rates in affected jurisdictions rose. Requires recognizing that longer sentences keep more people incarcerated (not released), so the released-offender pool is a biased sample of low-risk individuals.
stimulus: After several jurisdictions adopted mandatory minimum sentencing laws for repeat offenders, the recidivism rate among offenders released from those jurisdictions' prisons fell by 14 percent compared to pre-law rates. However, total violent crime rates in those same jurisdictions increased by 9 percent over the same period.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy in the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Mandatory minimum sentencing laws are politically popular in the jurisdictions that adopt them.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The mandatory sentencing laws kept a large population of high-risk, repeat offenders incarcerated for longer periods, while releasing primarily first-time or lower-risk offenders, whose recidivism rates were already low.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Prison conditions in the affected jurisdictions improved during the same period, which may have reduced the motivation to reoffend.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Some offenders subject to mandatory sentencing were convicted of nonviolent offenses.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Jurisdictions without mandatory sentencing laws also experienced increases in violent crime during the same period.

explanations.correct: If mandatory sentences kept the highest-risk repeat offenders incarcerated, those never released could not recidivate during the measurement period. The released pool thus consisted disproportionately of lower-risk individuals, artificially lowering the measured recidivism rate. Meanwhile, the large number of still-incarcerated high-risk offenders did not reduce crime that was already occurring, and the removal of deterrence for new first-time offenders may have contributed to the rise in total crime — reconciling both statistics.
explanations.A: Political popularity is irrelevant to the statistical discrepancy between recidivism and total crime rates.
explanations.B: Correct. Sample-composition bias explains the recidivism drop, and the continued absence of deterrence for new offenders explains the crime rise.
explanations.C: Improved prison conditions could explain lower recidivism but does not explain why total crime increased — this resolves one horn only.
explanations.D: Nonviolent offenders under mandatory sentencing is a tangential detail that does not reconcile the two statistics.
explanations.E: If other jurisdictions also saw crime rise, this context suggests an external cause but does not explain the simultaneous recidivism drop in the affected jurisdictions — this resolves one horn only.

difficultyReason: Arts/economics paradox: ticket prices for a regional theater rose substantially yet total revenue fell. Resolution requires understanding that demand is price-elastic in this market (higher prices drove away enough attendees to reduce total receipts).
stimulus: The Haverford Regional Theater raised average ticket prices by 25 percent in an effort to increase revenue and fund building renovations. In the season following the price increase, however, total ticket revenue fell by 11 percent compared to the previous season, even though no competing theaters had opened in the area.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy in the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Season-ticket subscribers, who purchased tickets at a locked-in rate, accounted for a majority of the theater's revenue in the previous season.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Attendance at the theater fell by 29 percent after the price increase, as many patrons chose to stay home or substitute other leisure activities.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The theater had planned to use renovation funds to attract higher-profile productions that would command premium ticket prices.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Theater attendance across the country declined modestly during the same season due to an economic slowdown.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Building renovation costs had increased significantly since the theater first announced its pricing strategy.

explanations.correct: A 29-percent drop in attendance means that even at 25 percent higher prices, total receipts (price × quantity) fell — because the percentage loss in quantity exceeded the percentage gain in price. This identifies the elastic-demand mechanism that reconciles the two facts: prices rose, yet revenue fell.
explanations.A: Season-ticket subscribers at locked-in rates would buffer revenue against price increases rather than explain a revenue fall; this may even deepen the paradox.
explanations.B: Correct. The attendance collapse quantitatively accounts for why higher per-ticket prices still produced lower total revenue, resolving both horns.
explanations.C: Future programming plans are irrelevant to the revenue outcome already observed — this resolves neither horn.
explanations.D: A modest national attendance decline is insufficient to explain an 11-percent revenue drop following a 25-percent price hike at a theater without new competitors; this resolves one horn only.
explanations.E: Rising renovation costs affect spending, not revenue, and are irrelevant to the discrepancy.

difficultyReason: Ethics/policy paradox: a charity that reduced its administrative overhead percentage saw a drop in donor contributions. Resolution involves a measurement-artifact/reverse-causation explanation: donors use overhead ratio as a quality signal, and a suspiciously low ratio triggered distrust.
stimulus: A well-known charitable organization reduced its administrative overhead from 18 percent of total expenditures to 6 percent, a figure that independent auditors confirmed as accurate. Nonetheless, annual donations to the organization declined by 22 percent in the two years following the announcement of this improvement.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy in the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Donors who give to charitable organizations generally prefer that most of their contributions go directly to the stated cause rather than to administration.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Major donors and watchdog groups interpreted an overhead ratio as low as 6 percent as implausible, concluding that the organization was likely underreporting expenses, and consequently withdrew their support.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The organization announced the overhead reduction through a press release that received wide media coverage.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Charitable giving in the organization's primary funding region declined by approximately 5 percent over the same two-year period.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The reduction in administrative overhead was achieved partly by reclassifying some administrative costs as program expenses.

explanations.correct: If donors and watchdogs saw the 6-percent figure as implausibly low and inferred fraudulent accounting, their rational response would be to withdraw contributions — explaining the donation decline despite (and because of) the announced improvement. The very accuracy of the figure was unpersuasive, resolving both horns through a reverse-causation trust mechanism.
explanations.A: This explains why donors generally prefer low overhead, making the donation decline more paradoxical rather than less — it deepens the paradox.
explanations.B: Correct. Perceived implausibility of the improvement triggered donor distrust, reconciling genuine overhead reduction with declining donations.
explanations.C: Wide media coverage would, if anything, be expected to increase donations by publicizing the improvement; this deepens rather than resolves the paradox.
explanations.D: A 5-percent regional decline in giving cannot account for a 22-percent drop in donations to one specific organization; this resolves one horn only and insufficiently.
explanations.E: If this were true, the auditor-confirmed figure would be misleading — but the stimulus states auditors confirmed accuracy. This answer contradicts the stimulus rather than resolving the paradox within its given facts.
